options: A mismatch between an index's logical (b-tree) order, which stays correct, and its physical order on disk, caused by page splits from inserts/updates/deletes
A permanent corruption of the index that only DBCC CHECKDB can detect
The index losing rows due to a failed transaction
A setting that must be manually enabled before an index can be queried
questions.explain: The b-tree stays logically correct; fragmentation is purely a physical-order-on-disk problem caused by page splits.

questions.q: Why does the lesson filter sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats results to page_count > 500 before acting on fragmentation percentage?
options: A small index fits in a handful of reads regardless of fragmentation, so its fragmentation percentage doesn't translate into meaningful extra I/O
The DMV returns inaccurate percentages for small indexes
SQL Server refuses to rebuild indexes under 500 pages
page_count has no real relationship to whether fragmentation matters
questions.explain: Fragmentation only costs real I/O once an index is big enough that physical layout actually determines how many pages a scan touches.

questions.q: What is the real trade-off between ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD and ALTER INDEX ... REORGANIZE?
options: REBUILD is thorough but resource-heavy (full sort, large log write); REORGANIZE is always online and lighter but only partially defragments the leaf level
They produce identical results with no difference in resource cost
REORGANIZE always outperforms REBUILD in every scenario
REBUILD cannot run online under any circumstance
questions.explain: REBUILD drops and recreates the index for a full defrag; REORGANIZE walks the leaf level in place, lighter and always online, but less complete.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call the '5-30% reorganize, 30%+ rebuild' guideline a starting point rather than a law?
options: Because the right choice also depends on table size and traffic — a small quiet table may not be worth a rebuild even above 30%, and a huge hot table might use REORGANIZE more often specifically to avoid REBUILD's resource spike
Because the percentages are randomly generated by SQL Server each time
Because REORGANIZE is always the correct choice regardless of fragmentation level
Because fragmentation percentages are not measurable in practice
questions.explain: The rule of thumb is a reasonable default, but real workload size and traffic patterns can justify deviating from it.

questions.q: Why is 'when' and 'which option' to rebuild/reorganize a real cost decision specifically on Azure SQL Database or Managed Instance?
options: Because index maintenance consumes the same metered CPU, IO, and log throughput that the application workload is paying for, so a poorly timed or unnecessarily heavy rebuild can throttle or compete with paying traffic
Because Azure charges a separate, explicit fee only for running ALTER INDEX statements
Because index maintenance is free on Azure but expensive on-premises
Because Azure SQL Database does not support ALTER INDEX at all
questions.explain: On metered compute, a rebuild's resource spike is a cost and availability decision, not just a performance one — which is why REORGANIZE's lighter footprint is sometimes the right choice.
